name: Monte Carlo Dropout
description: Monte Carlo dropout estimates how uncertain a neural network is about each prediction. Dropout randomly switches off some of the network's units and is normally used only in training, but here it stays on at prediction time. Each forward pass (one run of an input through the network) therefore uses a different random pattern of units, and the input is run through typically tens to a hundred times. The average gives the prediction, and the spread across runs is read as epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty from the model's limited knowledge rather than noise in the data. The method approximates Bayesian inference, but the spread is an estimate whose reliability should be checked against held-out errors.

example_use_cases.description: Quantifying diagnostic uncertainty in medical imaging models by running 50+ Monte Carlo forward passes to detect when a chest X-ray classification is highly uncertain, prompting radiologist review for borderline cases.

An autonomous-driving team replays recorded camera footage through its object detector with dropout left on, and finds the scenes (night rain, unusual vehicles) where detections vary most between passes. It uses them to decide what data to collect and which scenarios to add to simulation testing.

A grid operator's demand-forecasting network, trained with dropout, is run 100 times each morning. Days on which the forecasts spread beyond the planners' tolerance are sent for human review before reserve capacity is booked.

limitations.description: The spread across passes reflects uncertainty about the model's parameters, not noise in the data that varies from input to input. An input in a very noisy region can still show a narrow spread, so a narrow spread does not mean the outcome is predictable.

Each prediction needs many forward passes, typically 50 to 100, so inference costs that many times more compute, and too few passes make the spread itself unstable. The passes can run in parallel, which limits added delay but not total compute, so real-time or edge deployments with tight budgets may not afford it.

The network must have been trained with dropout, and the derivation assumes it sits before every weight layer. A model trained without dropout has to be retrained, so the technique is often unavailable for models already built or bought in.

The size of the spread depends on the dropout probability and weight decay, which the developer sets or tunes on validation data rather than learns from the data. The uncertainty scale is partly a design choice and needs checking against held-out errors.

The spread is an approximation, and its behaviour depends on the architecture. In the original paper's regression experiments, uncertainty kept growing away from the training data with ReLU activations but stayed bounded with TanH, so a narrow spread on unfamiliar inputs is not proof of familiarity.

resources.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
resources.abstract: Deep learning tools have gained tremendous attention in applied machine learning. However such tools for regression and classification do not capture model uncertainty. In comparison, Bayesian models offer a mathematically grounded framework to reason about model uncertainty, but usually come with a prohibitive computational cost. In this paper we develop a new theoretical framework casting dropout training in deep neural networks (NNs) as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes. A direct result of this theory gives us tools to model uncertainty with dropout NNs -- extracting information from existing models that has been thrown away so far. This mitigates the problem of representing uncertainty in deep learning without sacrificing either computational complexity or test accuracy. We perform an extensive study of the properties of dropout's uncertainty. Various network architectures and non-linearities are assessed on tasks of regression and classification, using MNIST as an example. We show a considerable improvement in predictive log-likelihood and RMSE compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and finish by using dropout's uncertainty in deep reinforcement learning.

Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

resources.title: Exploring uncertainty measures in deep networks for Multiple sclerosis lesion detection and segmentation

sample_claims.text: On held-out chest X-ray cases, the classifier's error rate among the 10% of cases with the highest Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty is at least double its error rate on the remaining cases.
The fraud model's Monte Carlo dropout variance is higher on transaction types held out of training than on types it was trained on, in a held-out check run before deployment.
Object detections flagged as high-uncertainty by Monte Carlo dropout are missed or mislabelled more often than unflagged detections when recorded driving scenes are replayed offline.
